The American Revolution. From seventeen seventy-five to seventeen eighty-three, the colonial uprising against British rule created the United States of America. Ignited by grievances over taxation without representation and British military occupation, the thirteen colonies unified under the Continental Congress and Continental Army to declare independence in seventeen seventy-six and secure it through eight years of armed conflict, succeeding against overwhelming odds and establishing a republic founded on Enlightenment principles of individual rights and popular sovereignty.

Tensions exploded after the Stamp Act in seventeen sixty-five and the Townshend Acts in seventeen sixty-seven, which imposed taxes on colonial goods without colonial representation in Parliament, sparking the rallying cry no taxation without representation. The Boston Massacre in seventeen seventy crystallized colonial opposition when British soldiers fired on protesters, and the Boston Tea Party in seventeen seventy-three saw colonists destroy a shipment of tea to protest the Tea Act. Lexington and Concord in April seventeen seventy-five marked the first military engagements, when British regulars attempted to seize colonial arms and were repelled by local militiamen.

The Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson in July seventeen seventy-six, articulated the philosophical case for independence and listed grievances against King George the Third. George Washington led the Continental Army through eight years of warfare, winning crucial victories at Trenton in seventeen seventy-six and Yorktown in seventeen eighty-one while enduring catastrophic winters at Valley Forge. The French, seeking to weaken Britain, entered the war in seventeen seventy-eight, providing naval power and troops that proved decisive at Yorktown, and Benjamin Franklin secured the alliance through diplomacy in Paris.

The Treaty of Paris in seventeen eighty-three formally recognized American independence and established the United States as a sovereign nation. The Revolution inspired republican and democratic movements worldwide, especially the French Revolution, and its ideas shaped the United States Constitution and the Bill of Rights.
